ISSUE
Public Hearing to adopt Joint Resolution No. CC 2022-066, SA 2022-004, HA 2022-001,
IDA 2022-001, PAA 2022-001, PCA 2022-002 and PFA 2022-001, approving the Annual
Operating and Capital Improvement Budget for Fiscal Year 2022-23.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that:
   The City Council, Chairs, Commissioners, Members and Directors conduct a
  public hearing to adopt Joint Resolution No. CC 2021-058, SA 2021-005, HA
  2021-002, IDA 2021-001, PAA 2021-001, PCA 2021-002 and PFA 2021-002,
  approving the Annual Operating and Capital Improvement Budget for Fiscal Year
  2022-23, and approving revenue and expenditure adjustments to Fiscal Year
  2021-22;

BACKGROUND
Each year the City is required to adopt a budget for the operation of the City. The budget
serves as the City’s financial plan for the Fiscal Year beginning July 1 through June 30.
It defines City priorities for the provision of services to the community.

According to the Palmdale Municipal Code: Chapter 3.04 Budget Adoption Procedures,
the City Manager shall submit a proposed budget to the City Council no later than May
31st of each year. Additionally, the City Council shall conduct a public hearing on the
proposed budget before adoption and shall adopt a budget prescribing the spending
 Report to Mayor and City Council, Chairs, Commissioners, Members, and Directors

policy of the City for the ensuing fiscal year on or before the thirtieth day of June of each
year.

On May 11, 2022, the Library Board of Trustees reviewed the proposed budget made a
unanimous recommendation to the City Council to approve the proposed Library budget.

On May 12, 2022, the Planning Commission unanimously found that the proposed
Capital Improvement Program is consistent with the goals, objectives, and policies of
the General Plan.

On May 18, 2022, the City Council was presented with a draft of the proposed Annual
Budget for Fiscal Year 2022-23.

On May 25, 2022, the Measure AV Oversight Committee was presented with a draft of
the proposed Measure AV budget for FY 2022-23 and provided feedback and a
recommendation for approval.

DISCUSSION
Staff is bringing forth the Proposed Budget for Fiscal Year 2022-23 for your review and
consideration.
As the City continues to recover from the impacts of Covid-19 pandemic, staff have
remained focused and committed to providing quality programs and services to our
residents. In alignment with the City’s adopted Strategic Plan, below is a list of program
highlights planned for FY 2023:
    Reinstated and expanded recreation activities, venues and events
    Community grant programs
    Continued food distribution programs at SAVES
    Investment in infrastructure
    Expansion of illegal dumping and graffiti clean-up efforts
    Housing Element implementation
    Permanent Local Housing Allocation Plan
    Waste Diversion – organics processing to comply with SB 1383
    Emergency management
    Film and Tourism programs
    Enhanced staffing levels to manage programs and to ensure a high level of
  customer service for our community

PERSONNEL
With the need to maintain and enhance certain services, additions to personnel are
necessary. The table below provides a summary of proposed personnel actions:

  $4,000 for eligible full-time employees and $500 for eligible part-time employees.
  Prorated rates may apply.
    Premium pay for qualifying Lifeguard staff proposed to be funded by American

  sustain retention and offered additional lifeguard certification classes, Palmdale

  o  700 hours - $500
  Eligibly period: Retroactive from May 1, 2022 through September 30, 2022

GENERAL FUND
Revenues
  1. Property Taxes are anticipated to increase by 4.6% due to property values
  increasing.
  2. Sales Taxes are expected to increase by 4.8% based on economic
  performance in the City.
  3. Charges for services are expected to increase by 35% as a result of Parks &
  Recreation programs being reinstated, as well as an increase in processing and
  planning fees.
  4. Other revenues are expected to increase dramatically, by 189%, in FY 2023 as
  a result of a one-time economic development property sale.
Expenditures
  1. Salaries and benefits are expected to increase by 3% (2% COLA and 1% wage
  increase) to employees. Other increases in the General Fund are a result of
  new positions proposed in FY 2023.
  2. LA County Sheriff Contract is expected to increase by 5.5% per the existing
  contract. The cost of the contract is proposed to be covered by multiple funding
  sources, including ARPA and Measure AV to relieve some burden from the
  General Fund. There is no increase in services or change in scope proposed in
  this budget. Amounts proposed are to maintain existing levels of services.
  3. LA County Sheriff Contract Liability is expected to increase by 11.5%, or
  $364,200.
  4. Transfers to Reserves for FY 2023 include:
  a. Pension Trust Fund to stabilize fluctuations in CalPERS rates: $1.25
  million
  b. Fleet maintenance to fund ongoing replacement of the City’s fleet:
  $250,000
  c. Information Technology to fund the ongoing upgrade of the City’s
  technology infrastructure: $250,000
  d. Drytown Waterpark to fund the ongoing capital costs relating to
  maintenance and improvements of the park: $500,000
  e. Park Development to establish healthy reserves in the event the City
  chooses to fund large projects in the future: $2 million

Fiscal Year 2022 was the first full year generating revenue through Measure AV. It
was initially estimated that Measure AV would generate $15.5 million in revenues from
the ¾ cent sales tax that was passed by voters in November 2020, however, sales tax
outperformed expectations and is now estimated to generate $21.9 million for FY

AMERICAN RESCUE PLAN ACT FUNDS (ARPA)

American Rescue Plan Act. The City received the first of two disbursements of funds in
July 2021, with the second disbursement expected before the end of FY 2022. U.S.
Department of Treasury released the Final Rule on April 1, 2022, implementing the
statutory provisions on eligible and ineligible uses of funds.

SPECIAL REVENUE FUNDS
Special Revenue and other funds consist of transportation funds, grants, and other
forms of restricted funding. Use of money in certain funds are governed by
memorandums of understanding, contracts, or law. Required audits are conducted
each year to ensure compliance with granting agencies.
One of the largest sources of revenue used by the City to pay for maintenance, repair,
and improvement of streets and facilities is transportation funding. These are sales tax
revenues that are collected by the State or County and allocated to the City based on
a percent of population.

CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT PROGRAM
The proposed FY 2023 Capital Improvement budget consists of a variety of projects
totaling $98.8 million. Many of the proposed projects are funded by grants or other
restricted funds. It is also important to keep in mind that capital projects are often a
multi-year effort, and therefore the budget established will carry through the life of the
project and may not be fully expended in the single year shown. The attached
schedules provide a comprehensive listing of all previously approved and proposed
capital improvement projects.

CONCLUSION
The proposed FY 2022-23 Budget is balanced and represents the City’s commitment to
the long-term planning and sustainability of programs and services for the community.

FISCAL IMPACT
The Fiscal Year 2022-23 Operating Budget will serve as the financial guideline for
program implementation for the year. The proposed annual budget is compliant with all
Financial Policies, including the 20% General Fund Reserve Requirement, with a 30%
reserve proposed in the budget. It is anticipated that revenues will be sufficient to
cover the expenditures proposed.

STRATEGIC PLAN
Goal II: Ensure long-term fiscal health of the City and maintain funding for services.
  B. Manage resources, costs, and liabilities to ensure the City’s long-term fiscal
  health.
  C. Involve and expand engagement to enhance public oversight and
  transparency.

 City Council
The City Council is the governing body of the City of Palmdale with direct responsibility for formulating City
policies, enacting laws, and deciding land use issues. The City Council also serves as the Successor Agency
to the Redevelopment Agency, Palmdale Airport Authority, and Palmdale Civic Authority governing board. The
City is divided into five (5) geographic areas, and voters in each district elect one council representative who
also lives in that district. The five-person council designates one of its members to serve as Mayor at the
December meeting each year. Additional information on voting districts is provided on the City’s website at
www.cityofpalmdale.org/Elections.
The City Council’s duties include approval of the Annual Budget and oversight of financial affairs of the City.
The Mayor and City Councilmembers appoint the City Manager and the City Attorney. The City Council has the
power to adopt ordinances and resolutions; make appointments to advisory boards and commissions; establish
policy and approve programs; act on program and administrative recommendations of City staff; appropriate
funds and approve contracts; and provide direction to staff in response to concerns and needs of residents and
businesses, as well as advocating for/against local, state and federal legislative and regulatory issues.
Staff to the City Councilmembers assist in responding to numerous calls and letters from citizens each week,
including conducting research and drafting responses.

FY 2022-23 Goals & Objectives
• Promote community engagement by establishing special public committees to address public safety, park
  safety, and the General Plan update;
• Remain steadfast in supporting economic development driven projects to stimulate job creation, business
  retention and economic growth;
• Continue effective outreach to support the local business community and develop a strategy for community
  recovery post COVID-19;
• Continue to promote the City’s values and leadership philosophy;
• Continue to implement the Ten-Year Capital Improvement Plan (CIP);
• Complete the redistricting process; and,
• Represent the City’s interest in regional, state, and federal issues.

The City Attorney’s Office provides representation and advice to the City Council and all City agencies,
authorities, boards, commissions, and all City officers and staff in all matters of law pertaining to the City.
The City Attorney acts as general counsel to the City Council and all City agencies, boards, committees, and
commissions. The City Attorney’s Office provides advice and direction to City staff related to the operation of
the municipal government, and reviews and prepares resolutions, ordinances, contract services agreements
and Public Works contracts as needed.

adjourned meetings of the City Council, Successor Agency to the Community Redevelopment Agency,
Palmdale Civic Authority, Housing Authority, Industrial Development Authority, Airport Authority, Planning
Commission, Mobile Home Rent Control Board, and Library Board of Trustees, and hearings (upon request);
draft or review all ordinances, resolutions or agreements presented to the City Council and its agencies,
boards and commissions (as needed); coordinate all pending litigation pertaining to the City; remain available
at all times for consultation and advice on legal matters by the City Council, City Manager or City staff; and
supervise insurance and risk management matters for the City.

Debt Service
Debt Service is a series of payments of interest and principal required to be paid on a debt over a given period
of time.
The City’s debt management policy provides for the City’s current and future ability to finance major operating
capital equipment and capital improvement projects at beneficial interest rates without adversely affecting the
City’s ability to finance essential City services.
Decisions regarding the use of debt are based upon, but not limited to, factors such as economic,
demographic, and financial resources available to repay the debt, the City’s long-term operating and capital
needs, review and analysis of financial strength ratios and indicators, and the impact of future debt financing
on these ratios and indicators.
The types of debt covered in this section are notes payable, certificates of participation bonds, revenue bonds,
lease revenue bonds, and capital leases.
The City issued a variable rate note by entering into a Department of Housing and Urban Development
contract for Loan Guarantee Assistance under Section 108 of the Housing and Urban Development Act of
1974. The City received advanced proceeds and used the proceeds for property acquisition, relocation, and
demolition costs associated with the development of the proposed Legacy Commons for Active Seniors.
The City entered into a purchase and sale agreement with Southern California Edison for streetlight acquisition
in the amount of $11.6 million, $11.4 million of which was financed by Opus Bank.
The City entered into a capital lease for the copiers throughout the City with a payment term of five years.
Subsequently, the City entered into additional capital leases for two copiers with payment terms of 42 months
and 32 months, respectively. Debt service information on the capital lease can be found in the Information
Technology section of City Manager programs.
The City entered into a 13 year lease purchase agreement to finance the acquisition of energy efficient
equipment.
Certificates of participation bonds were issued by the Palmdale Financing Authority per assignment
agreement, by and between the City and the Authority. The Palmdale Financing Authority issues the debt and
then loans the proceeds to the City to finance the acquisition, construction, or refinancing of public capital
improvements. Lease payments are made pursuant to a lease agreement and are sufficient to pay principal
and interest on the bonds as due.
Certificates of participation bonds were issued by the Palmdale Civic Authority. The Palmdale Civic Authority
issues the debt and then loans the proceeds to the City to finance public improvements of the City. Certificates
of participation allow the public to purchase participation in a stream of lease payments relating to the
acquisition or construction of specific equipment, land, or facilities. Lease payments are made pursuant to a
lease agreement and are sufficient to pay principal and interest on the certificates as due.
Lease revenue bonds are issued by the Palmdale Financing Authority. The Palmdale Financing Authority
issues the debt and then loans the proceeds to the City to finance the acquisition, construction, or refinancing
of public capital improvements. Lease payments are made pursuant to a lease agreement and are sufficient to
pay principal and interest on the bonds as due.
The Housing Authority of the City of Palmdale issued multifamily housing revenue bonds to finance the
acquisition of multifamily housing facilities.

Building and Safety
The Building and Safety division administers plan review and inspection services for all construction requiring
building permits within the City. It provides interpretation and enforcement of applicable California building and
City municipal codes and is also responsible for issuance of building permits and Certificates of Occupancy.
The division registers, inspects, and certifies all rental properties within the City; investigates and resolves
building and housing issues from residents, businesses, and developers; and performs post-disaster safety
assessments.
The Building and Safety division:
• Provides digital plan checks through the ProjectDox system;
• Provides virtual video inspections via Google Duo, FaceTime, or Zoom as requested by our customers;
• Provides online applications for all permits, including online permitting for water heaters and heating and air
  conditioning permits;
• Processes over the counter permits for simple building permits and pools, patios, signs, roofs, electrical,
  plumbing, mechanical and sewer permits;
• Provides solar inspections;
• Provides next-day inspections with a two-hour inspection arrival window and courtesy calls to each
  inspection requestor to provide them this time frame, therefore decreasing waiting time for the customer on
  the jobsite;
• Publishes a daily inspection schedule on the Building & Safety page of the City’s website; and,
• Responds to records requests from the public concerning historical permit data and plan copies.

Engineering
The Engineering division includes the Civil Engineering and Public Works Inspection sections. The Civil
Engineering section is responsible for the development and implementation of engineering standards for

capital improvement projects. The Public Works Inspection section is responsible for inspecting all building

Maintenance sections. The Traffic/Transportation section is responsible for conducting traffic studies for the
installation of traffic control devices; reviewing land development project applications as it relates to traffic and

transportation providers to meet community needs; designing roadway improvements, signage, bikeways and
traffic signals to promote the safe and orderly movement of vehicular, pedestrian and bike traffic as well as
goods; providing support to school districts on their suggested Routes to School programs. The Traffic Signal
and Street Lighting section is responsible for maintaining and coordinating preventive maintenance for the
City’s existing traffic signals, existing citywide traffic signal single mode fiber optic network, and the citywide
street lighting system. They also maintain, under an agreement with Los Angeles County, several Los Angeles
County traffic signals and school flashers located within and near the City of Palmdale.

Park Maintenance
The Park Maintenance division cares for City parks and facility grounds, general benefit landscapes, park and

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-065 a Resolution of the City Council of the City of
Palmdale restating in its entirety the Palmdale Master Schedule of Fees and Repealing
Resolution No. CC 2021-057.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-065 to authorize the proposed fees and charges
  for the fees, charges, and requirements set forth in the City of Palmdale Master
  Schedule of Fees for Service, effective July 1, 2022, and attached hereto;

  2. Repeal Resolution No. CC 2021-057;

BACKGROUND
Periodically, the City Council adopts Fee Resolutions, which 1) revise existing fees,
rates, or charges; 2) establishes new fees, rates, or charges; or 3) revise headings or
descriptive language for existing fees for the City's operating departments.

On June 15, 2021, the City Council adopted Resolution No. CC 2021-057 adopting a
citywide fee schedule that was to be implemented in a biennial phased in approach, with
some increases taking effect July 1, 2021 and some taking effect July 1, 2022.
Resolution No. CC 2021-057, Section 4 authorized proposed rates for Planning,
Engineering and Building & Safety, in a biennial phase approach.

Additionally, The 2021-22 fee schedule was reformatted and as part of that process
some information from the previously adopted 2017 Fee Schedule was unintentionally

omitted. Upon thorough review, the proposed Master Schedule of Fees has corrected
this matter, restoring missing fees and policies.

DISCUSSION
The State Constitution provides the authority for cities to impose user fees and
regulatory fees for services and activities, however the fees may not exceed the
estimated reasonable cost of providing the service or performing the activity.

In order to better achieve the City’s policy regarding cost recovery goals and to minimize
General Fund subsidies for services provided staff has identified inefficiencies, missing
fees and/or processes.

Staff recommends that the City Council adopts Resolution No. CC 2022-065 to authorize
proposed adjustments to the Palmdale Master Schedule of Fees for certain departments
detailed in this staff report and presented in the attached Master Schedule of Fees,
effective July 1, 2022.

PARKS AND RECREATION

DryTown has two new rental items, glow in the dark inner tubes for evening events and
smaller sized shade cabanas. Both of these items have been added to the fee schedule.
With the CPI increase last year, cabana pricing for the larger units were changed to an
odd figure. For marketing purposes, this fee is proposed to be slightly reduced. Similarly,
for marketing and efficiency all fees have been increased to the nearest .25, which has
historically been the practice. Fees and policies from the 2017 Fee Schedule which
were unintentionally omitted in subsequent schedule updates have been restored.

One omitted policy, which defines how recreation program fees are to be established
has been updated to reflect current recommendations, trends and practices. A
recommendation from the user fee study conducted by Revenue & Cost Specialists,
LLC suggested that the City Council develop a conscious policy as to what programs
should be subsidized with tax monies in promoting social benefit and to what extent.
Likewise, current industry best practices have shifted to a subsidy and cost recovery
policy, titled pyramid methodology by BerryDunn.com and GreenPlay LLC. This
methodology originated in the 1990’s and is now widely practiced across the United
States. The resulting pyramid model illustrates appropriate program subsidy levels and
cost recovery targets, which provides the framework necessary for decision making.
The bottom of the pyramid consists of basic services free to the public in the interest of
social and community benefit. The top of the pyramid consists of services that are
structured, specialized or are used by special interest groups or individuals. Services at
the bottom of the pyramid are subsidized by City revenues, conversely services at the
top of the pyramid are incrementally off-set by participation fees. Reference Fee
Schedule attachment, Parks & Recreation Cost Recovery Pyramid.

The City has historically charged a 5% GIS fee on various Building & Safety, Planning
and Engineering fees to recoup the City’s GIS cost, which include software and labor
required to track and maintain locations of any and all permits, assets and any additional
items that have a geographical location within the City. Extensive staff time is required
to maintain accurate GIS information, which is then used by City staff and the public for
purposes of permitting, plan check, inspections, engineering and various aspects of
planning. The public is also provided limited access to the City’s GIS data, which aids in
the application processes. See Exhibit J, attached.

ECONOMIC & COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT
Building & Safety and Planning divisions are proposing to add an Expedited Fee for the
below services. The inclusion of this fee in the City’s Master Schedule of Fees is a
response to the developer community and the desire to have the option to request and
pay for an expedited turnaround time on services. This is an optional fee.

Exhibit A – Building & Safety
   Expedited Plan Check

Exhibit O - Planning
   Expedited Conditional Use Permit (CUP)
   Expedited Preliminary Project Review to Development Advisory Board (DAB)
   Expedited Site Plan Review

NEIGHBORHOOD SERVICES
There are no proposed changes to fees in the Neighborhood Services section of the
Master Schedule of Fees, however, additional language has been added to show the
specific code violations that are subject to administrative citations, as well as the City’s
policies for handling repeat violations, late payments and collections. See Exhibit K,
attached.

CONCLUSION
Any action by the City to levy a new fee or service charge or to approve an increase in
an existing fee or service must be approved by ordinance or resolution. Before any new
fee or service charge can be added to the Palmdale Fee Resolution, a public hearing
must be held, and reasonable notice must be provided to the members of the
community.

As such, Staff recommends that the City Council Adopt Resolution No. CC 2022-065
and Repeal Resolution No. CC 2021-057, authorizing the proposed fees and charges

Definitions:
1. Agencies with proof of Internal Revenue Code IRC 501 (c) (3) (4) (5) and (6) are considered non-profits.
2. Commercial use is defined as an event held for the purpose of generating monetary gain for the event sponsor(s).
3. Direct program costs are exclusively incurred as a result of the program and are frequently variable, adjusting as program participation
  varies. Direct cost examples include part-time personnel, supplies, contract services and equipment.
4. Indirect program costs that are shared among several programs and are necessary to execute general day-to-day operations. Indirect
  cost examples include personnel overhead, utilities and custodial expenses. Indirect costs are not considered as fees and charges
  are determined.
Policies
1. Non-profit with verifiable status of IRC 501 (c) (3) (4) (5) or (6) are eligible for a 25% facility reservation rate reduction. Unless otherwise
  specified, facility reservation fees that are eligible for a rate reduction are noted by an 8. Rate reductions do not apply to personnel fees,
  facility deposits or equipment rental.
2. Unless otherwise specified, the rate for use of facilities for commercial purposes shall be charged at 200% of the hourly reservation fee,
  in addition to 5% gross admission ticket sales and gross alcohol sales. These fees may be reduced or waived if the applicant can
  demonstrate that residents of the City of Palmdale benefit from the use of facilities or the services being provided.
3. Unless otherwise specified, set-up and clean-up charges are comprised of applicable facility hourly reservation rates.
4. Park parking lots are generally not available for exclusive use reservations. If exclusivity can be accommodated and if parking fees are
  charged by the renter, 25% of parking fees collected are to be paid to the City.
5. Parks & Recreation program and service fees are established by following specified cost recovery policies. Fees and charges are
  determined by identifying direct costs if providing services and apply the cost recovery goals stated below. Direct program costs are
  referenced in the definitions section. It is widely accepted that park and recreation systems are publicly financed, and therefore offer free
  or affordable services. The level of program subsidy will be based on an assessment of the community or social benefit, local market and
  economic conditions. As services have a greater appeal to individuals or groups of individuals, it is appropriate to charge fees for the
  services at an increasing rate of cost recovery. Cost recovery target categories include: Community Benefit/Access, free; Community
  Benefit, 0-25%; Balanced Beneficiaries, 25-50%; Substantial Individual Benefit, 50-75%; Exclusive Individual Benefit, 75-100%.
  Cost recovery categories are further defined in Exhibit L-1.
General Fees
1. Unless otherwise specified, a special event application processing fee of $250 may be charged for staff services required to process the
  application, which may include coordination with other City departments, or State and County government agencies. The fee is
  non-refundable and does not guarantee approval of the application.
2. Unless otherwise specified, fees for personnel shall be calculated at hourly rate for staff wages, plus 45% for full-time benefits or 15%
  for part-time benefits and a 25% administrative fee. Unless the use warrants otherwise, staff will be scheduled to be on-site
  one-half hour before and after use.
